title: Attractions.io partners with Bosque de Chapultepec on new guest app
summary:
Attractions.io, a leading creator of mobile visitor apps, has partnered with Bosque de Chapultepec, a vast park in Mexico City that includes nine museums, a castle, and a zoo. Together, the organisations have developed a new guest app that helps guests explore the 866-hectare site.

At almost three times the size of Central Park, Bosque de Chapultepec is often best approached as a collection of attractions, with several visits needed to simply see the highlights.

Visitors at Bosque de Chapultepec can explore multiple atttractions across four different sectionsImage courtesy of Attractions.io

In a site this vast, wayfinding tools and staff can only do so much to point visitors toward their chosen attractions, let alone reveal the park's hidden corners.

As such, the park needed a unified digital experience that could orient visitors across all four of its sections in real time, even with limited phone signal.

This experience needed to help visitors plan their day based on their interests and available time, discover what's on (including exhibitions, events, and seasonal activities), and reach visitors directly with updates, reducing the reliance on physical signage.

The resulting app helps guests navigate the complex site with confidence, garnering 30,000 downloads per month and a 4.9-star rating on the App Store.

Data-backed decision-making

The team partnered with Attractions.io to create a brand-new mobile app that uses interactive maps and GPS wayfinding to help visitors move between sections and surface points of interest, facilities, and food options as they explore.


Aldair Contreras, digital manager, Bosque de Chapultepec, says: "We have hundreds of activities, but they're often not in a fixed location; they might be in the forest or out on the grass.

"Having accurate points of interest has helped our guests find activities more easily, as well as helping them discover new experiences they didn't know about when they arrived."

More than 150 unique activities are now discoverable and promoted through the app. These range from historic monuments to free activities such as yoga sessions or watercolour workshops, many of which had never appeared on a printed map.

Data from the app also informs which activities are recommended to visitors while on site. With these recommendations, guests can build a plan around their interests and the time they have available, which also reveals hidden attractions they might otherwise miss.

For example, following major investment, funfair attendance failed to grow as anticipated. The team found that the barrier to attendance was awareness rather than appeal, and is using the app to overcome this challenge.

"International guests didn't know we had a funfair, and locals didn't know it had reopened," says Natasha Uren Vázquez, executive director, Bosque de Chapultepec.

"Now we have the app, we're promoting it more, and attendance has been rising steadily."

Precise communications

In addition to enhancing the visitor experience, the app offers a live picture of how guests explore, and the data has become one of the park's core tools for deciding where to invest.

"The reports we get from our app management console have been so important in helping us plan and grow for the future," says Natasha Uren Vázquez, executive director, Bosque de Chapultepec.

"We now know that 60% of our guests spend most of their time at a single location and are looking into investing more to improve that specific space."

These findings helped support a funding application for the long-overdue refurbishment of the park's dining areas, with the app's user data providing evidence on how many visitors were using those spaces.


Guests can use the new Bosque de Chapultepec app to plan their visit around their own interests and availabilityImage courtesy of Attractions.io

Bosque de Chapultepec also plans to use the app for location-targeted advertising.

As a public body, the park has to be mindful of how often and when it reaches out to visitors. With the app, messages can be sent only to relevant visitors. This can alert nearby app users, for example, that a yoga class starts in ten minutes, rather than broadcasting to the entire audience.

This precision allows the park to directly promote free events and festivals to visitors, rather than relying on social and local media reach.

Recently, Attractions.io helped drive food and beverage revenue by introducing mobile food ordering at Chester Zoo, the UK's most-visited wildlife attraction.

title: Beyond the kiddie coaster
summary:
While theme and amusement parks have traditionally offered attractions for different age groups, operators are increasingly adding family rides that let different generations experience them together. Instead of watching while their young child rides, parents and grandparents can share the experience.

For operators, these attractions offer an opportunity to create shared experiences for families visiting together, allowing children and adults to experience the same attraction rather than being separated by height or age requirements.

This has contributed to growing interest in family coasters and other attractions designed to appeal to a broad age range.

ART Engineering, Lagoon Amusement Park and Potts Park offer examples of how ride engineering, operator-manufacturer collaboration and accessibility are influencing the development of family attractions.

​Opening coaster experiences to a wider demographic


For family attractions, minimum height requirements are an important consideration for operators and manufacturers.

Minimum height requirements are determined by factors including ride design, restraint systems, and applicable safety requirements, and they can determine which family members can ride together. Many coasters require riders to be at least 100 cm, 110 cm or 120 cm tall, excluding young children eager to graduate from flat rides.

ART Engineering, which has been developing innovative roller coasters, dark rides, carousels, and water rides since its founding in Kirchzarten, Germany, in 2003, has made the 90 cm (32 inches) height requirement a cornerstone of its family portfolio.


By engineering a system that lets children measuring just 90 cm ride safely when accompanied by an adult, the company has opened its coaster experiences to an entirely new demographic.

Georg Behringer, managing director of ART Engineering, says operators are increasingly looking to create attractions that multiple generations can experience:


"Many of our clients focus on families as their target customers, aiming to provide a shared experience for family members of all ages. Our family roller coasters are designed according to that focus. The seats and restraint systems are suitable for small children and also offer comfortable accommodation for large adults.

“Combined with a dynamic—though not overly aggressive—ride experience, this ensures a fantastic time for all ages"

Designing a vehicle and restraint system that can securely accommodate both a child and an adult presents a significant engineering challenge. The physical differences mean that a lap bar fitting snugly against an adult's thighs could create a hazardous gap over a child's lap.

To overcome this, ART Engineering has developed seating and restraint systems designed to accommodate a wide range of rider sizes, including systems that close from above or secure the lap individually, adapting dynamically to different body shapes and sizes without sacrificing passenger comfort.

"We put a great deal of effort into developing the seat,” says Behringer. “The goal was to ensure that both small passengers and large adults could sit safely and comfortably. To achieve this, we conducted extensive tests with a wide range of people.

“The result is that a baseball player can now ride our roller coasters together with their three-year-old child."

​Braus & Saus at Potts Park


For Potts Park, a family-oriented amusement park in Minden, Germany, introducing a roller coaster that could cater to very young children while still offering an exciting ride experience was a key goal. The result was Braus & Saus, a custom-designed Family Shuttle Launch Coaster from ART Engineering.


Park owner Henrik Pott explains that the decision of manufacturing partner came down to trust and a willingness to iterate on the design:

"A key reason to choose ART is the relationship of trust involved in the collaboration. For our roller coaster, ART kept iterating the layout until we had the best solution. We recall going through eight different versions. The Wild Stone Age themed area found its fitting finale with the Braus & Saus attraction.

"The ride’s alignment with the heartline is superb, making the entire experience a real pleasure."

Repeated design iterations allowed the teams to refine the layout and the forces riders experience. The track is designed around riders' centre of gravity (the "heartline"). This alignment ensures that transitions, banks, and curves are smooth, eliminating lateral jolts and jerks that could otherwise scare or discomfort a young child.


In a park where families with young children are the primary demographic, offering a high-speed, dynamic-launch coaster for families is a significant competitive advantage.

"Most of our attractions are accessible to children from three years of age when accompanied by an adult. Beyond that, many guests are impressed that Braus & Saus is also open to riders from three years of age,” says Pott.

Pott says the combination of the ride experience and theming has also contributed to its appeal:

"Visitors are absolutely delighted with Braus & Saus. Feedback has been universally positive, with many guests immediately getting back in line for another ride. People particularly highlight the "farting" mammoths and the ride's smooth operation."

The success of Braus & Saus shows that a family coaster is not just about the physical track, but about the storytelling and the joy it brings. "Ultimately, the overall storytelling and its execution determine an attraction's success. It is difficult to point out just one element.

“What we value most about working with ART is our shared commitment to creating the best possible product and their availability to make necessary optimisations even after the ride has launched."

Primordial at Lagoon


Meanwhile, at Lagoon Amusement Park in Farmington, Utah, the same focus on family audiences was applied on a much larger scale with Primordial, an award-winning interactive coaster and dark ride hybrid.

In 2023, Lagoon opened this themed, interactive family coaster, representing one of the most ambitious engineering undertakings in the park's history. It features a custom-built mountain, interactive shooting elements, slow-moving dark ride sections with rotating gondolas, and sudden drops.


Dustin Allen, Lagoon's director of engineering, says that Primordial filled a spot in the park’s attraction lineup that was missing, adding: “The guest reception has been fantastic, with queue lines today continuing to prove the ride’s popularity three years after opening.

“In fact, Lagoon had to alter the park opening to accommodate the number of guests going directly to Primordial at “rope drop”, as well as changing ride operation closing policies to support the popularity of the ride."

Allen details the collaborative spirit that made ART Engineering a good fit for the ambitious project:

"The design, manufacture, installation, and commissioning of Primordial required very intricate communication and coordination. Relationships with the several companies involved in the project were crucial to the success of the ride.

“Lagoon has partnered with ART Engineering for several projects throughout the years (including the Cannibal and Bombora rides), and that relationship of trust and cooperation was solid.”

Primordial represented an evolution of the interactive coaster concept.

Although ART Engineering had previously developed similar dark ride/coaster hybrid technology for Canada's Wonderland with the Wonder Mountain's Guardian attraction, the concept for Primordial was developed further through new train designs, interactive targeting, and additional physical coaster elements.

“ART Engineering had proven to be more than capable of tackling these challenges and did so with distinction.”


Allen says the attraction has also had an impact on Lagoon's attendance:

“Park attendance has grown each year since the announcement of that ride. Many comments have been received about the upgrades to the amusement park in recent years, with Primordial being a prime example of Lagoon going above and beyond the expectations of the guests in providing world-class rides and attractions.”

Additionally, Primordial received multiple national and international recognitions, including an IAAPA Brass Ring Award, USA Today Reader’s Choice Award, and placing in blooloop’s Innovation Awards.

The recognition has also helped attract visitors from outside the local region, he adds:

"Primordial changed both the landscape (figuratively and literally, we built a mountain for this ride!) and the perception of what Lagoon – a regional park in Utah – is able to provide as an experience for our guests."

​​From kiddie coasters to new adventures


One of ART Engineering's greatest strengths is its diversified family ride portfolio. Its range includes traditional lift coasters alongside launch, shuttle, and interactive concepts, allowing operators to choose different ride formats based on available space and the desired experience.

At the entry level is the Kiddie Coaster, designed specifically for the youngest riders. This model, a gentle introduction to coaster kinetics, can be found at leading theme parks such as Europa-Park in Germany and Legoland Windsor in the UK.


The classic Family Coaster is the company's signature model. Featuring either a traditional chain lift or a friction wheel lift, this coaster incorporates thrilling, family-friendly track elements while utilising a low FRP (fibre-reinforced plastic) shell so children over 90 cm have a clear, unobstructed view from every seat.

This classic model has been installed at parks like Nigloland in France.

The portfolio has also expanded into launch and shuttle formats, including the Family Launch Coaster, Family Spike Launch Coaster and Family Shuttle Launch Coaster. These designs introduce acceleration and changes in direction while retaining the lower height requirements associated with family attractions.


Family Coaster from 90cm height restriction:

  • Kiddie Coaster
  • Family Coaster
  • Family Launch Coaster
  • Family Shuttle Launch Coaster
  • Family Spike Launch Coaster incl. switch track
  • Family Duelling Launch Coaster (coming in 2027)
  • Family Thrill Coaster

Controlled rotating coaster (4 seats in a row):

  • Adventure Coaster
  • Adventure Interactive Coaster

Coaster with inversions:

  • Mega Coaster


At the start of 2026, ART Engineering relaunched its Adventure Coaster product category. Building on the lessons of interactive ride engineering, the Adventure Coaster represents a step forward in personalised storytelling. It debuted as the Galacticoaster at Legoland Florida and Legoland California.

Galacticoaster also illustrates the shift towards more interactive coaster experiences, with riders able to configure their digital spacecraft before boarding.


"The feedback has been consistently positive,” says Behringer.

“The Legoland Galacticoaster combines a fantastic ride experience with show effects. Riders are immersed in the story right from the queueing area. This approach creates a personalised experience for the rider, going beyond mere theming."

The Adventure Coaster uses four-seat vehicles and a central boarding platform, a layout designed to keep groups together during the experience.

​Across the thrill spectrum


While family-friendly attractions are a major focus for ART Engineering, the company’s engineering capabilities also extend to extreme thrills, for example, the iconic Cannibal mega coaster at Lagoon.

"Cannibal is the result of close collaboration with Lagoon,” says Behringer. “The goal was to create a unique roller coaster offering intense thrills and inversions.”

Opened in 2015, Cannibal features an enclosed vertical tower lift, a 110-degree nose-dive drop, and the high-speed Lagoon Roll inversion.


Allen adds: "Cannibal really put Lagoon on the map. Bombora [a custom family coaster] was the first collaborative coaster with ART Engineering and set the stage for the ambitious Cannibal, Lagoon’s second collaborative coaster. Cannibal became the tallest and fastest ride in the park when it opened.

“With the unique tower lift system, it also became an iconic landmark for the park. It is loved by guests for its smooth track, unique elements, and consistently moving queue line (the ride regularly hits the theoretical capacity of 1200 PPH).

“Possibly Cannibal’s greatest attribute is the operational uptime and consistency. Through the first ten seasons of operation, the ride was able to open each day that the park opened. There were days that the ride was operational only for a short time, but there was never a full day where guests were left without the opportunity to ride the marquee attraction."

Cannibal's operational record also highlights the importance of reliability and long-term performance alongside ride design and engineering.

​Long-term reliability with ART Engineering


For operators making a multi-million-dollar investment in a new coaster, long-term reliability is as important as the initial ride experience. When an attraction is out of service, guest satisfaction falls, queue times at other rides lengthen, and the park's overall reputation suffers.


Behringer says ART considers long-term operation during design and development, supported by post-launch service.

"The customer invests in a product intended for long-term use. ART Engineering's goal is to deliver quality. To achieve this, the product's lifespan requirements are considered throughout the development process. Careful component selection, comprehensive quality management, and our ongoing service are prerequisites for a successful product lifespan."

An extensive parts & service programme underpins this dedication to quality.

Looking ahead, Behringer expects family coaster designs to continue developing.

“I think family roller coasters will continue to evolve—with new ride elements, more extensive theming, and greater customisation,” says Behringer. “New manufacturing processes are being implemented, and AI may increasingly play a role in certain processes."

​The evolution of the family coaster


The examples of Potts Park and Lagoon illustrate how the family coaster category is expanding beyond traditional children's attractions, with operators and manufacturers exploring lower height requirements, more sophisticated ride systems, and greater interactivity.


For operators considering a next-generation family coaster, Henrik Pott's advice is to start with the intended audience and the fit between the attraction and the park:

"Pay attention to your target audience and ensure the ride is a good fit for them. If the ride has already been installed elsewhere, try it out for yourself."

As the distinction between family and thrill attractions becomes less defined, the family coaster category is likely to continue evolving. For operators, the challenge is not simply to lower the minimum height requirement, but to create an experience that works for different ages, confidence levels, and expectations within the same attraction.

Attendees at IAAPA Expo Europe 2026, taking place in London from 22 - 24 September, can meet the ART Engineering team at booth #S803, where they can learn more about the company's roller coaster projects.

title: Universal sets opening date for Fast & Furious coaster
summary:
Universal Studios Hollywood has announced the opening date for its new Fast & Furious roller coaster.

Fast & Furious: Hollywood Drift, the theme park's first high‑speed outdoor coaster, will open to guests on Wednesday, 16 September.

The fastest coaster in Universal's lineup, reaching speeds of up to 72 mph, Hollywood Drift has been undergoing technical rehearsals and previews for the past month.

Fast & Furious Hollywood Drift opens at Universal Studios Hollywood on 16 September, marking its official debutUniversal

Based on Universal Pictures’ Fast & Furious film franchise, the attraction features state-of-the-art ride technology and a unique dual-launch split-ride track.

The 4,100-foot aerial track will take riders over and under sections of the Starway escalator, as well as through an inverted dive loop, a twisted pretzel loop and an inverted stall, among other elements.

The ride will also offer panoramic views of the San Fernando Valley, the Universal Studios movie studio and the theme park.

Riders will travel in one of four Fast Saga vehicles, the Dodge Charger, Mazda RX-7, Nissan Skyline GT-R or Toyota Supra, each based on cars driven by characters in the Fast & Furious films.

Each vehicle can rotate independently through 360 degrees and features its own engine and sound effects to simulate a high-speed street race.

- YouTube www.youtube.com

In what Universal describes as a "technological first", part of the Fast & Furious Hollywood Drift track will run through a transparent section of the queue, giving guests a glimpse of the coaster as they wait to ride.

Last month, Universal Hollywood announced plans to install two additional sound barriers around its new Fast & Furious coaster in response to noise complaints.

In a statement to The Independent, a spokesperson for Universal Studios Hollywood said: "Community feedback has been an important part of our testing process and in response to that feedback, we are implementing additional sound-reduction measures to further lessen sound levels in the adjacent neighbourhood."

Universal Orlando will also debut Fast & Furious: Hollywood Drift in 2027.

title: How to choose & budget for the right trade association for your attractions business
summary:
Choosing which industry association to join is one of the most critical decisions an attractions operator or supplier can make.

With limited budgets, competing global markets, and an array of niche and generalist trade bodies, businesses must evaluate where their money—and, more importantly, their team’s time—will generate real-world returns.


In Part 1 of this two-part guide, we explore how to evaluate organisational fit, balance regional vs. international scopes, and calculate the true long-term value of your membership dues.


  • Mission fit beats features lists: The strongest membership ROI starts with aligned values and long-term organisational fit, not just a transactional checklist of perks.
  • Look beyond the trade show floor: While annual conventions draw the crowd, the true return on investment accumulates year-round through workforce credentials, market intelligence, and public advocacy.
  • Evaluate scope strategically: Don't judge an association by its geographical label alone. Regional, national, and international memberships serve distinct, complementary purposes.
  • Membership is an active investment, not a subscription: You cannot passively subscribe your way to industry influence. The greatest return demands active volunteerism, committee participation, and peer knowledge-sharing.
  • Ask three core questions before paying: Assess your current growth stage, your 3-to-5-year ambitions, and your internal capacity to participate before committing your budget.

​Defining organisational fit: mission, workforce, and personal value


Finding the right association is rarely about picking the biggest name in the directory; it begins with aligning your business goals with the organisation's core purpose.

When an organisation’s mission aligns with the association’s, the relationship shifts from a transactional agreement to a mutually supportive partnership.

The triple fit for membership:

  • Mission fit: Shared values, sustainability goals, conservation, and policy advocacy.
  • Workforce fit: Staff training, professional development, credentials, and industry standards.
  • Personal fit: Finding a community of peers, mentorship, inspiration, and personal leadership growth.

For Melissa Howerton of the Association of Zoos & Aquariums (AZA), finding the right fit starts with a shared mission. While AZA commercial members receive a full suite of marketing, networking, and information-sharing benefits to reach decision-makers, the deepest value comes through dedicated active involvement.


The AZA Commercial Member Engagement Council (CMEC) offers vendor members high-level access to the AZA Board, allowing suppliers to act as strategic partners sharing expertise directly in sustainability, diversity, conservation, and technology.

When an organisation’s mission aligns with the Association’s, membership becomes more than a transaction—it becomes a mutually supportive partnership.— Melissa Howerton, AZA

Beyond high-level strategy, fit must also serve daily operational needs.

Sarah Joyce of the Audiovisual and Integrated Experience Association (AVIXA) urges businesses to evaluate associations through a workforce development lens.

A key consideration is whether an association offers practical training, market intelligence, and globally recognised credentials—such as AVIXA's Certified Technology Specialist (CTS) programme.

These credentials build internal team expertise while proving technical credibility to prospective clients.

Adding a human perspective, Nicola Hamilton of Ecsite (the European network of science centres and museums) says that organisational fit is deeply personal.

Companies may join to support strategic priorities, but individual staff members engage because an association fits their personal aspirations—whether seeking a peer network, professional development, or fresh inspiration.

The core question to ask is: Who will help us solve our problems and deliver the real-world impact we seek to create?

Affiliation choices also send a powerful message externally. As Natanya Khashan of the American Alliance of Museums (AAM) says, membership signals to clients that a business is actively invested in understanding the sector and staying current on emerging issues.

Meanwhile, Ming Yang of the China Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions (CAAPA) advises evaluating an association's network breadth alongside your current stage of growth.

A company seeking investment or distribution should prioritise organisations with strong resource-matching capabilities; CAAPA, for instance, connects members across cultural tourism, commerce, sport, agriculture, public culture, and technology.

​Balancing limited budgets: regional, national, or international scope?


When trade budgets are tight, deciding whether to invest locally, nationally, or globally can be daunting. However, lower dues should never be the sole deciding factor.

Balancing geographical scope:

  • Regional & national organisations: Provide invaluable local networking, market-specific insights, direct regulatory guidance, and policy advocacy. Best for establishing immediate domestic footholds.
  • International associations: Offer exposure to global innovation, emerging trends, global best practices, cross-border partnerships, and international benchmarking. Essential for global technology, design, and overseas expansion.

Howerton warns against letting price dictate alignment, noting that even a low-cost membership is a wasted investment if the association's connections and year-round benefits don't fit your immediate growth targets.

The decision to join internationally is not necessarily about organisational maturity; it's often driven by the ambitions of the people involved. — Nicola Hamilton, Ecsite

While national bodies excel at local advocacy and regulatory guidance, Hamilton says that joining an international network is driven by a team's ambition to innovate, benchmark internationally, and build cross-border collaborations—regardless of company size or maturity.


In technology-driven fields, industry conversations are inherently global. As Joyce highlights, access to an international network lets members learn from digital transformation and visitor engagement projects in other markets before those innovations become mainstream in their own region.

Flexible membership tiers can help businesses test international scope while managing tight budgets.

Regional and national memberships can also act as complementary layers: regional groups build deep local relationships, while national organisations surface macro trends and connect you with national leaders. Khashan says that using both levels strategically provides full coverage.

Ultimately, Yang advises looking past official labels altogether. National bodies like CAAPA regularly organise events with a global outlook and international networking capacity, whereas some international labels may lack practical service delivery.

The true metric is whether the organisation's actual activities match your current development stage.

​Calculating ROI: trade shows vs. year-round value


While trade shows are a primary reason many companies join associations, relying solely on floor leads during a busy three-day exhibition is an outdated approach to calculating return on investment.

The shift in event ROI strategy:

  • The traditional exhibitor approach: Short-term sales focus, gathering quick lead lists on the show floor, and a transactional "sell, sell, sell" mindset.
  • The modern partner approach: Demonstrating field-tested expertise, solving buyer challenges, building long-term trust, and engaging year-round in committees.

Approaching events as a peer rather than just a seller yields far greater returns. Howerton says that while leads are gathered on the show floor, long-term relationships are forged in session rooms, hallways, committee meetings, and informal conversations throughout the event.

Exhibitors build trust by serving on committees, speaking on panels, and contributing knowledge to discussions.

Exhibitors should not treat trade shows merely as places to gather sales leads. They should see them as starting points for building long-term trust. — Ming Yang, CAAPA

With buyer decision-making cycles and project developments taking much longer today, Yang says that trust in a supplier’s team and delivery capacity is rarely established during a single trade show. It requires continued communication, ongoing service, and consistent visibility.

To support this, associations are actively redesigning event spaces to foster relationship-building over transactions.


Khashan says that introducing dedicated digital media lounges, food stations, and a puppy park at AAM's Annual Meeting encouraged attendees to linger in the Expo Hall, resulting in 80% of museum CEOs meeting directly with an exhibitor.

Furthermore, during AAM's Museums Advocacy Day, Industry Partners advocate directly alongside museum leaders with policymakers, demonstrating that a strong museum sector drives economic activity—an experience partners rate as one of their most valuable membership benefits.

Listening to client challenges allows sales leads to follow naturally.

Joyce emphasises the critical year-round support associations provide outside of trade shows, including workforce initiatives like the AVIXA Foundation, sustainability benchmarking via AVIXA's Sustainability Advisory Group, and market intelligence research to help navigate economic uncertainty.

​Cross-sector convergence: breaking down industry silos


As the boundaries between theme parks, museums, zoos, science centres, and immersive technology providers continue to blur, trade associations are actively building bridges between previously isolated sectors.

Sectors converging across attractions:

  • Theme parks & attractions: Adapting immersive technology, storytelling, and custom content.
  • Zoos & aquariums: Partnering on conservation education, sustainability, and green technology.
  • Museums & science centres: Integrating interactive guest experiences, digital displays, and multi-sensory storytelling.
  • Retail, sports & public spaces: Adopting experiential entertainment models and destination content.
  • Immersive technology (AV): Driving underlying digital transformation across all venue types.

Cross-sector learning helps organisations discover fresh approaches to visitor engagement.

Joyce says that AVIXA fosters this exchange through educational programmes, councils, and initiatives like the Brad Sousa Impact Fund, which encourages direct collaboration between audiovisual technology and digital transformation communities.

This crossover creates rich mutual benefits across disciplines. Khashan says that museums learn operational and guest-experience strategies from attractions, while cultural organisations contribute deep expertise in education, storytelling, and community engagement.

Cross-sector collaboration is also embedded in organisational partnerships.

Howerton says that at the AZA Annual Conference, members can earn continuing education credits through external bodies like the Association of Fundraising Professionals or the American Association of Zoo Veterinarians, while ongoing exchanges with the American Public Gardens Association help share best practices across adjacent sectors.


For suppliers, cross-sector integration drastically expands addressable markets.

Yang highlights CAAPA's decade-long push for cross-sector initiatives—including "cultural tourism + agriculture", "cultural tourism + technology", "cultural tourism + sport", and "cultural tourism + museums".

Equipment manufacturers and content providers who previously served only traditional theme parks now find major opportunities in public cultural spaces, urban parks, and commercial venues.

​3 questions to ask before committing your budget


To wrap up, our expert panel leaves operators and suppliers with a clear framework for allocating their 3-to-5-year membership budgets.

The 3-question membership audit (CAAPA framework):

  1. Development stage: What stage of growth is our business currently at?
  1. Future goals: What are our specific development targets for the next 3 to 5 years?
  1. Resource capacity: How much budget, time, and personnel can we realistically commit to active participation and committee service?

Adopting a long-term mindset is essential. Hamilton challenges leadership to evaluate whether an association supports people at all levels of your business—from emerging professionals to senior leaders.


View this post on Instagram

A post shared by AZA (@zoos_aquariums)

Similarly, Howerton says that a membership investment is only as valuable as the internal effort put into it. Companies must ask if they are genuinely prepared to volunteer, serve on committees, and share expertise before signing up.

Membership fees should not be viewed simply as an operating cost. They should be considered a strategic investment in resource connections, brand development, market expansion and long-term industry relationships. — Ming Yang, CAAPA

​Coming up in Part 2...


You've selected your association and paid your annual dues—now how do you extract maximum return on investment?

In Part 2, our expert panel breaks down step-by-step strategies for onboarding team members, navigating committee appointments, leveraging year-round research, and converting association involvement into tangible business growth.

title: Stage secrets: 3 lessons every theme park can learn from theatre
summary:
What do theme parks and theatre have in common? More than one might think! Both are built around delivering a unique experience, and both are considered successful when audiences keep coming back for more.

That connection is exactly why I believe theme parks as a whole have a lot to gain by watching and studying how theatre companies craft space for audiences.

Below are three lessons theatre can teach theme parks, based on my work across numerous departments on immersive experiences, theatrical productions, and mixed media installations.

1. Serve the story first, the technology second

The first lesson is to ensure creative storytelling remains a singular priority throughout the process, from ideation to installation. Storytellers are as old as humanity itself, so it's no surprise that theatre as a craft has a pretty sharp sense for this.

Theatrical audiences are eager to repeatedly ask “why” as a core experience of attending productions, and critics (especially in NY) are waiting and ready to eviscerate shows over anything short of uninterrupted brilliance.

When working with live performers especially, authenticity and integrity are the rulers observers use to measure the quality of the performance they came to see.

While not a frequent occurrence, I have reasoned myself out of design teams, justifying why I shouldn't be there when producers focused too much on technology and gimmicks, thinking it would sell tickets and attract investors.

I believe that’s also the key to creating an amazing ride or guest experience. You have to know why the technology you've chosen will help serve the story you're trying to tell. If you can't answer that, the technology simply doesn't belong.

View this post on Instagram
A post shared by Universal Orlando Resort (@universalorlando)

Following theatrical convention, an audience should never be asked to “put these glasses on” or “get in this cart” unless it's an essential part of the journey. Turning a rollercoaster into a minecart race and recreating the harrowing jumps of the original SNES game with a side-mounted rail system is a brilliant example of this, as Epic Universe recently did.

Personally, I like the firework analogy.

Sure, you can do one brilliant firework, but then it fizzles, and it's gone. So many productions that fall short focus on creating one great firework moment, but fail to address how we got there, why we should care, or how to carry on after it fizzles away.

Executing all of these elements together while orchestrating how they combine and flow to create a cohesive journey even has a term: ‘Mise-en-scène.’

In the recent West End production of Hercules the Musical, the brilliant combination of LED screens and precision projection mapping gave audiences a sense of scale that physical scenery couldn’t achieve alone.

In Broadway’s Maybe Happy Ending, video content, lighting, and moving panels created a forced perspective for the audience, treated as a core narrative element rather than simply a backdrop. The digital and physical elements were so tightly integrated that audiences couldn’t tell where the physical set ended and the projection began.

When technology is driven by the narrative, it goes from feeling like a spectacle for spectacle’s sake and becomes an essential part of an emotional experience that keeps guests returning and reminiscing for years to come.

2. Don’t allow technology to break the fourth wall

In theatrical storytelling, breaking the fourth wall is a frequent and deliberate choice made by actors and directors.

However, if your technology is breaking this wall due to failure or glitches, it’s not overly dramatic to say you’ve shattered the magic, and all the hard work building a world literally vanishes. It’s the immersive equivalent to being told Santa Claus isn’t real.

In technical theatre, we often joke that if you don’t notice the work we did, we did our jobs right. We call achieving this effect the “willful suspension of disbelief,” and it is the currency we start to trade in when the lights start to dim on stage.

Sadly, I've seen attractions pushed past their limits with systems that were expected to run every day, in heat and humidity, for a decade or more. It's frustrating to watch rides deteriorate over time, especially when park teams don't have the tools to resolve issues quickly (even a re-ride line doesn’t provide guests with a complete experience).

Disney's Hercules - Mount Olympus & Muses Credit Johan Persson/© Disney

As rides become more technically complex, these late-stage failures become a serious engineering consideration.

When designing a technical solution, many take an approach that consolidates technology and hardware into as tight a box as possible: the “ubermensch approach.” However, doing this increases the risk of failure exponentially.

To avoid this, engineers have learned to distribute their core components and choose purpose-built infrastructure, so the story never ends. Modern theatre productions typically rely on server-grade components with built-in real-time redundancy, such as Disguise’s media servers.

If your primary system has an issue, a backup machine takes over without dropping a single frame, and no server relies on more than a single GPU – dedicating 100% of each server's resources to guaranteeing longevity and performance.

3. Design holistically

Unlike theatrical productions, which are often run by tight-knit teams that work on each part of the production process as a single group, theme park stakeholders are varied and numerous, so workflows are often spread across multiple departments and divisions.

This can be a problem because historical knowledge lives only in whatever handoff and documentation exists between creatives and operators once a ride is open. Park staff assumes ownership, and the engineers and designers who deployed the ride move on to the next project.

This is why I advocate for a persistent presence of a role found in the film industry: the production designer.

In UK theatre, this person is also called a theatre designer or scenographer. A technically minded production designer has the skills and knowledge necessary to oversee not just the commissioning and deployment of an attraction, but also to consider and leverage its upkeep.

Working with a resident or associate director helps theatre productions preserve the original creative team's work and keep shows running true to form through multiple recastings and remounts for extended runs.

The second edition of Dragone's groundbreaking immersive show, Terhal, uses Disguise technologies to power new content, projections, and a huge chandelier of LED screens Image credit: Dragone

Theatre also pushes the boundaries of what we even consider a ‘stage.’

A talented production team knows how to think about things from every angle when staging a production ‘in the round’ or overtaking found spaces for immersive theatrical experiences.

This is why working with a visual environment such as Disguise Designer is such an invaluable tool.

Iterating in a navigable, real-time 3D environment lets everyone visualise elements from every angle when crafting attractions and experiences, building confidence in creative concepts and allowing designers to previsualise nearly every component of a ride before breaking ground.

Theatre (the craft) has spent centuries refining the art of immersing audiences while balancing creativity, technology, and operational excellence to tell unforgettable stories. As theme parks continue to embrace more ambitious digital experiences, those same principles have never been more relevant.

Get the foundations right, and the technology becomes more than a spectacle – it becomes part of the story guests remember long after they've left the park.
